# The Time Machine – Fundamentals of Interest & Discounting

> "Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn't, pays it."
> — *Attributed to Albert Einstein*

Time is the most brutal constraint in economics.
A dollar today is not a dollar tomorrow. Why? Because you could have spent it (consumption preference) or invested it (opportunity cost).
Financial mathematics is nothing more than the architecture of time — a set of tools to transport value from the present to the future (**Compounding**) and from the future back to the present (**Discounting**).
In this chapter, we build the engine of finance.

## The Logic of Time: Why Money Has a Price

Before we calculate, we must understand.
Why do banks pay you interest? It is not charity. It is the *price of time*.
If you lend money to a bank, you defer your ability to spend it today. This sacrifice requires compensation.
Economically, the interest rate ($i$) is composed of three layers:

1. **Risk-free rate:** The pure price of time (consumption deferral). In the Eurozone, this is anchored to the European Central Bank base rate, reflected in market benchmarks like EURIBOR.
2. **Inflation premium:** Compensation for the loss of purchasing power.
3. **Risk premium:** Compensation for the danger that the borrower might default.

### The Trinity of Interest

* **Theory:** Liquidity Preference Theory (Keynes) suggests we prefer cash now over cash later — and must be compensated to give it up.
* **Norm:** Central banks set the reference rate (ECB deposit rate, Fed Funds Rate). Commercial rates are built on top, adding premiums for inflation and credit risk.
* **Practice:** In 2022, inflation in the Eurozone hit 10%. If your savings account paid 0.5%, your *real* interest rate was negative. You were paying the bank to hold your melting ice cubes.

The relationship between the nominal rate ($i_{nom}$), inflation ($\pi$), and the real rate ($r$) is the **Fisher Equation**. The approximation — valid when both rates are small — is:

$$r \approx i_{nom} - \pi$$

::: {.quick-check}
**Inflation Check:**
Your bank offers you a **5%** nominal interest rate per year. However, the current inflation rate is **7%**.
What is your approximate **real interest rate**?

- +2% (I am getting richer)
- **-2% (I am losing purchasing power)**
- 12% (Nominal + Inflation)

> **Calculation:**
> $$r \approx 5\% - 7\% = -2\%$$
> You are effectively paying the bank to hold your money while it loses value.
:::

::: {.flip-card}
#### Opportunity Cost
The benefit foregone by choosing one alternative over another. In finance, the opportunity cost of holding cash is the interest you *could* have earned — it is the rational foundation for demanding compensation over time.
:::

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The Silent Heist — Inflation in Turkey (2022)

In 2022, Turkish banks offered savings rates of **30% p.a.** to stop Lira holders from converting to Dollars. That sounds remarkable — until you check the other number.

**The Trap:** Inflation ($\pi$) in Turkey hit **85%** that year.

**Approximate (Fisher shortcut):**
$$r \approx 30\% - 85\% = -55\%$$

**Exact Fisher Equation** — necessary at extreme rates:
$$1 + r = \frac{1 + i}{1 + \pi} \quad \Rightarrow \quad r = \frac{1.30}{1.85} - 1 \approx -29.7\%$$

The approximation ($-55\%$) overstates the loss because inflation is so large. The shortcut is reliable for rates below roughly 10%; beyond that, use the exact form.

**The Verdict:** Whether approximate or exact, you lost purchasing power — fast. The nominal rate was a vanity metric.

> **Managerial Insight:** Always ask for the *real* rate. Only that buys you bread (or Porsches).
:::

## The Engine: Simple vs. Compound Interest

There are two ways to grow money. One is linear (boring), the other is exponential (explosive).

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
<iframe src="assets/Chapter1/effektzinseszins.html"
        style="width: 100%; height: 700px; border: none;"
        loading="lazy">
</iframe>
:::

### Simple Interest (The Linear Trap)

Simple interest is calculated *only* on the original principal — never on accumulated past interest. Each year adds the same fixed amount.

**Variables:** $FV$ = Future Value, $PV$ = Present Value (Principal), $i$ = interest rate (decimal), $n$ = number of periods.

$$\boxed{FV = PV \cdot (1 + n \cdot i)}$$

It is like a tree that grows new branches but never grows leaves on those branches — the annual increment is always the same.

> **When to use Simple Interest:** Short-term instruments only (typically $n < 1$ year): treasury bills, overnight deposits, supplier credit. For all multi-year investment decisions in this course, compound interest is the correct model.

### Compound Interest (The Exponential Beast)

Compound interest earns interest *on interest*. Every period, the accumulated balance becomes the new base.

$$\boxed{FV = PV \cdot (1 + i)^n}$$

The difference from simple interest seems trivial in Year 1 but becomes enormous over time.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Simple vs. Compound: $100 at 10 % for 3 Years
**Simple:** $FV = 100 \cdot (1 + 3 \times 0.10) = \$130$. **Compound:** $FV = 100 \cdot (1.10)^3 = \$133.10$. The \$3.10 gap looks small here — stretched over 30 years or larger sums, the compound engine dominates completely.
:::

> **The Rule of 72 (Mental Math Hack)**
> How long does it take to double your money? Divide 72 by the annual interest rate.
> * At 6%: $72 / 6 = 12$ years.
> * At 12%: $72 / 12 = 6$ years.

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The $24 Empire — The Manhattan Paradox

In 1626, Peter Minuit purchased Manhattan for trade goods worth approximately **$24**. Today, Manhattan real estate is worth trillions. Most people assume Minuit made the deal of the millennium. But did he?

**The Counter-Factual:** What if the Lenape had invested that $24 at a standard **6% compound interest**, reinvested annually for ~400 years?

$$FV = 24 \cdot (1.06)^{400} \approx 24 \cdot 13{,}200{,}000{,}000 \approx \$316 \text{ billion}$$

**The Verdict:** The exponential function at a *modest* 6% over four centuries creates wealth rivaling the GDP of small nations. Manhattan is valuable — but time is the more powerful force.

> **Managerial Insight:** You do not need a high return. You need *endurance*.
:::

::: {.drag-exercise}
In simple interest, capital grows *linearly*, meaning the absolute interest amount remains constant each year.
In compound interest, capital grows *exponentially*, because interest is *reinvested* to generate further returns in every subsequent period.
:::

## Time Travel: Compounding and Discounting

We have seen how to move money *forward* in time. But in investment appraisal, we almost always need to move money *backward*.

You pay for a machine **today** ($t = 0$). You receive the cash returns **in the future** ($t = 1, \dots, n$). To compare them, you must pull future values back into the present. This operation is called **Discounting** (Abzinsen) — the mathematical inverse of Compounding.

The interactive timeline below shows both directions on a single axis:

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
<iframe src="assets/Chapter1/zeitstrahl.html"
        style="width: 100%; height: 460px; border: none;"
        loading="lazy">
</iframe>
:::

### The Operation: Discounting (Abzinsen)

The discounting formula is simply the compound interest formula rearranged.

**Start from:** $FV = PV \cdot (1+i)^n$

**Divide both sides** by $(1+i)^n$:

$$\boxed{PV = \frac{FV}{(1+i)^n} = FV \cdot (1+i)^{-n}}$$

The factor $(1+i)^{-n}$ is called the **Discount Factor** (Abzinsungsfaktor). It is always smaller than 1 (assuming $i > 0$) — it shrinks the future value down to its present-day equivalent.

| Direction | Operation | Formula | Effect on value |
|-----------|-----------|---------|-----------------|
| $t_0 \to t_n$ | Compounding (Aufzinsen) | $FV = PV \cdot (1+i)^n$ | Grows |
| $t_n \to t_0$ | Discounting (Abzinsen) | $PV = FV \cdot (1+i)^{-n}$ | Shrinks |

::: {.drag-exercise}
In the discounting formula $PV = \frac{FV}{(1+i)^n}$, if the interest rate ($i$) increases, the Present Value *decreases*, because the denominator becomes *larger*.
This means: High interest rates punish *distant* future cash flows more severely than near ones.
:::

::: {.case-study}
#### Case: The $700 Million Illusion — Shohei Ohtani

In December 2023, Shohei Ohtani signed the largest contract in sports history with the LA Dodgers: **$700 million over 10 years**. The media celebrated. Financial analysts smiled.

**The Structure:** During his playing years (2024–2033), Ohtani receives only $2 million/year. The remaining **$680 million** is deferred to 2034–2043 — paid out at $68 million/year, with no interest.

**Discounting three of those deferred payments (at $i = 5\%$):**

| Year | Payment | Discount Factor | Present Value |
|:----:|--------:|:---------------:|-------------:|
| 2034 (t = 11) | $68 M | $(1.05)^{-11}$ | ≈ $39.7 M |
| 2038 (t = 15) | $68 M | $(1.05)^{-15}$ | ≈ $32.7 M |
| 2043 (t = 20) | $68 M | $(1.05)^{-20}$ | ≈ $25.6 M |

Every year of delay costs roughly 5 % of the payment's value. Summed across all ten deferred payments, the $680 million shrinks substantially.

**The Verdict:** The MLB Players' Union estimated the contract's Net Present Value at approximately **$460 million** — not $700 million.

> **Managerial Insight:** Ohtani gave the Dodgers a massive interest-free loan. The *timing* of a cash flow is just as important as its *size*.
:::

### Practical Example: The Lottery Choice

**Scenario:**

* **Option A:** € 1,000,000 cash today.
* **Option B:** € 1,100,000 in one year.

::: {.quick-check}
**Assume the interest rate is 15%. Which option should a rational investor choose?**

- Option B (more money is always better)
- **Option A (€ 1,000,000 today)**

> **Step-by-step:**
>
> **Step 1 — Discount Option B** to $t = 0$:
> $$PV_B = \frac{1{,}100{,}000}{1.15} \approx 956{,}521$$
>
> **Step 2 — Compare** at the same point in time:
> $$PV_A = 1{,}000{,}000 > PV_B = 956{,}521 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Choose Option A}$$
>
> The high interest rate makes waiting expensive. *At 5 % interest, Option B would win.*
:::

::: {.quick-check}
**You expect € 10,000 in 2 years. The interest rate is 10%. What is the Present Value?**

- € 8,000
- **€ 8,264.46**
- € 12,100

> **Calculation:** $PV = \dfrac{10{,}000}{(1.10)^2} = \dfrac{10{,}000}{1.21} \approx 8{,}264.46$
:::

::: {.details}
#### Deep Dive: Day Count Conventions
In academic theory, $n$ is measured in full years. In banking practice, it gets messier:

* **30/360 (German Method):** Every month is counted as 30 days (12 × 30 = 360). Simple but slightly inaccurate.
* **act/act (ICMA):** Actual calendar days in the period divided by actual days in the year. Used for Euro-government bonds and interest-rate derivatives.

For this course, unless otherwise stated, assume $n$ is measured in full years.
:::
